identity.name: Republic of Indonesia
alt_names: Republic of the United States of Indonesia

land.text: Java, Madura and Sumatra, the land of which the Netherlands later recognised the Republic as the de facto authority (Linggadjati, November 1946); the whole of the Dutch East Indies after 27 December 1949 except western New Guinea

predecessors.note: The Dutch East Indies had been occupied by Japan from 1942; the Proclamation of 17 August 1945 came two days after Japan's surrender. Cliopatria draws Japan over the islands in 1943-1945 and starts the Republic in 1946.

capitals.name: Jakarta
capitals.note: The Republic's first seat; the page says the Dutch landed there with British help and 'could not hold the city', and the Republican leadership then settled in Yogyakarta, without dating the move.

capitals.name: Yogyakarta
capitals.note: The Yogyakarta page: it 'became the capital of the Indonesian Republic from 1946 to 1948'; the Dutch invaded Yogyakarta in Operation Kraai (19-20 December 1948) and the capital moved to Bukittinggi 'on 19 December 1948'. The Revolution page dates neither the move to Yogyakarta nor the return to Jakarta.

capitals.name: Bukittinggi
capitals.note: The Yogyakarta page: the capital was moved to Bukittinggi 'on 19 December 1948'; the Revolution page puts the Emergency Government (PDRI) in West Sumatra. The president and vice-president were exiled to Bangka.

capitals.name: Yogyakarta
capitals.note: The Roem-Van Roijen page: 'On 6 July, republican leaders Sukarno and Hatta returned to the capital' after the final Dutch forces left the Yogyakarta region on 30 June 1949. The pages do not date the move back to Jakarta; the state's capital is Jakarta from 1950 (Indonesia page).

capitals.name: Jakarta
capitals.note: Capital throughout; the page mentions Nusantara in East Kalimantan as the future capital planned since 2022.

correction.text: the Republic proclaimed on 17 August 1945: Java, Madura and Sumatra with Aceh, the land the Netherlands recognised as its de facto authority at Linggadjati

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria starts the Republic in 1946. The page gives no boundary for 1945; the 1946 shape (Java and Sumatra) is borrowed for the proclamation year at confidence 2. Reviewer fix: Aceh is added because Cliopatria's 1946 shape holds only 55 of its 184 cells (it draws the rest as a Sultanate of Aceh row, marked wrong in sultanate-of-aceh). Aceh page: 'The ulama won, and the area remained free during the Indonesian War of Independence' and 'The Dutch military itself never attempted to invade Aceh' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aceh).

569,148 km2: Java (Jakarta only half) and Sumatra except most of Aceh. Linggadjati, 'concluded in November 1946', recognised 'the Republic as the de facto authority over Java, Madura, and Sumatra'; the shape fits that apart from Aceh, which Cliopatria cuts out as its own Sultanate of Aceh row for 1946-1948 and so holds only 55 of Aceh's 184 cells (13,910 of 46,534 km2). Reviewer fix, verdict ok to adjust: Aceh is added back, since Aceh page: 'The ulama won, and the area remained free during the Indonesian War of Independence' and 'The Dutch military itself never attempted to invade Aceh' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aceh). sultanate-of-aceh marks its 1946, 1947 and 1949 rows wrong and sends them to this dossier. No infobox area exists for the Republic of 1946.

correction.text: Java (Jakarta only half), Madura and Sumatra including all of Aceh, the land the Netherlands recognised as the Republic's de facto authority at Linggadjati

keyframe_review.note: 408,209 km2 for 1947-1948 after Operation Product: West Java gone, half of Central and East Java kept, Sumatra reduced. The page: Dutch forces drove the Republic out of 'parts of Sumatra, and East and West Java' and 'The Republic was confined to the Yogyakarta region of Java'; the Renville Agreement (ratified January 1948) froze the Van Mook line, 'an artificial line which connected the most advanced Dutch tanks' positions'. Reviewer fix, verdict ok to adjust: the 1947 shape holds only 54 of Aceh's 184 cells; Aceh is added back. Aceh page: 'The ulama won, and the area remained free during the Indonesian War of Independence' and 'The Dutch military itself never attempted to invade Aceh' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aceh).

correction.text: the Republic after Operation Product: central Java and Sumatra with all of Aceh, which the Dutch never invaded

union.text: the guerrilla Republic of 1949: the Riau and Jambi pocket plus West Sumatra, seat of the Emergency Government, plus Aceh, which the Dutch never invaded

minus.text: western New Guinea, kept by the Netherlands

union.text: from 27 December 1949: all the former Dutch East Indies except western New Guinea, as in ledger 15

correction.text: the guerrilla Republic of 1949 (the Riau and Jambi pocket, West Sumatra and Aceh) and, after the transfer of sovereignty on 27 December 1949, all the former Dutch East Indies except western New Guinea: the shape the state has at the end of 1949

keyframe_review.note: 122,120 km2 for 1949: Riau, Jambi and only 9 percent of West Sumatra. The page says the Emergency Government 'was established in West Sumatra' after Kraai (19 December 1948), so West Sumatra is added. The Roem-Van Roijen agreement (7 May 1949) and the Dutch withdrawal from Yogyakarta (30 June 1949) are now in the ledger as a gain of the Yogyakarta region in 1949-06 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roem%E2%80%93Van_Roijen_Agreement); the shape here is the year's guerrilla pocket. The 1949 shape ends on 26 December; on 27 December 1949 the whole Dutch East Indies except western New Guinea passes to the state. Reviewer fix: the 1949 shape holds none of Aceh's cells, so Aceh is added. Aceh page: 'The ulama won, and the area remained free during the Indonesian War of Independence' and 'The Dutch military itself never attempted to invade Aceh' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aceh). fx-27 review: the compiler applies a keyframe at the end of its year, after the ledger, so the pocket-only shape stripped the 27 December 1949 transfer (ledger 15) again and the 1950 keyframe had to add 4,459 cells (Kalimantan, Sulawesi, most of Sumatra) in one jump; the transfer region is added to the shape. Indonesian National Revolution page: 'Sovereignty was formally transferred on 27 December 1949' and the state 'would include all the territory of the former Dutch East Indies with the exception of Dutch New Guinea' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesian_National_Revolution).

minus.text: western New Guinea (Papua and West Papua), which the Netherlands kept in 1949

correction.text: the Republic of the United States of Indonesia, then the unitary Republic, without western New Guinea

keyframe_review.note: 2,022,994 km2 against the infobox 1,904,569 km2 (ratio 1.06): the shape reaches 140.96 E, so it contains western New Guinea, which the Netherlands kept ('transferred sovereignty, excluding western New Guinea'). It is removed until 1 May 1963. The state is the Republic of the United States of Indonesia from 27 December 1949 and a unitary republic from 17 August 1950 (the Indonesia page: 'replaced by a unitary republic on 17 August 1950').

correction.text: the Republic without western New Guinea and with Aceh, which Cliopatria draws as its own row in 1953-1959; Aceh is the Darul Islam contest zone from 20 September 1953 (ledger), the government holding the towns

keyframe_review.note: 1,981,051 km2: the 1950 shape minus about 70 percent of Aceh (Cliopatria's Sultanate of Aceh row, 1953-1959) and still including Papua. Aceh was Indonesian territory in rebellion: on 20 September 1953 Daud Beureu'eh 'declared Aceh part of the Islamic State of Indonesia', and Darul Islam 'controlled more than 90%' of Aceh in 1957, the government holding the towns; the ledger carries Aceh as a contest zone against negara-islam-indonesia, as it does West Java and South Sulawesi, which stay inside the shape. Reviewer fix: Aceh is added back to the corrected shape and western New Guinea is removed.

correction.text: the Republic without western New Guinea; holds 1960-1962, the Papua keyframe of 1963 follows

keyframe_review.note: Holds only for 1960-1962: the Netherlands kept western New Guinea until the New York Agreement (15 August 1962), UNTEA's administration and the transfer to Indonesia on 1 May 1963. Aceh returns to the shape (98 percent of it) in 1960 because Cliopatria's Aceh row ends in 1959, although the Darul Islam peace in Aceh is dated 1959-1962 on the Darul Islam page.

correction.text: the Republic with western New Guinea from 1 May 1963; Indonesian rule formalised by the Act of Free Choice in 1969

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: the 1960-1975 Cliopatria shape is right from 1 May 1963 ('UNTEA then transferred the territory to Indonesia on 1 May 1963'); 'The Act of Free Choice in 1969 formalised Indonesian rule' (Indonesia page).

correction.text: the Republic with East Timor, annexed as the 27th province on 17 July 1976; holds 1976-1998 only

keyframe_review.note: 2,041,331 km2 for 1976-2005 including East Timor (93 percent of Timor-Leste). The page: 'On 17 July 1976, Indonesia formally annexed East Timor as its 27th province'; the last Indonesian troops left by 31 October 1999, so the shape holds only to 1998. The Cliopatria East Timor row starts in 2006 and leaves 1999-2005 (UN administration, independence 20 May 2002) to a new east-timor keyframe.

correction.text: Indonesia without East Timor after the UN took over in October 1999

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria keeps East Timor in the Republic to 2005 although 'By 31 October 1999, the last Indonesian troops had left East Timor' and 'independence was declared on 20 May 2002'. The 2006 shape is used for 1999-2005.
2,023,107 km2 against the infobox 1,904,569 km2 (ratio 1.06, within the factor of two): the outline is the modern archipelago. No border change since 1999 on the pages opened.
Same outline as 2006; nothing on the page changes the border in 2024.

region.text: Java, Madura and Sumatra: 'the Republic as the de facto authority over Java, Madura, and Sumatra' (Linggadjati, November 1946) (with all of Aceh, which Cliopatria cuts out of its 1946 shape)

ledger.note: 1945: Sukarno and Hatta proclaim Indonesian independence (17 August), two days after Japan's surrender. The page gives the date; the core is the researcher's reading of the Linggadjati recognition (Java, Madura, Sumatra), for the Dutch East Indies were in Japanese hands. Reviewer fix: Aceh is added to the region. Aceh page: 'The ulama won, and the area remained free during the Indonesian War of Independence' and 'The Dutch military itself never attempted to invade Aceh' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aceh).

region.text: Jakarta, Medan, Padang, Palembang, Semarang and Surabaya, the Republican cities where British forces, with Dutch NICA troops, landed (mirrors dutch-east-indies /ledger/97 and /ledger/99)

ledger.note: October 1945: British forces, with Dutch NICA troops, land in the Republic's cities. 'The first British troops reached Jakarta in late September 1945'; British forces reached Medan, Padang, Palembang, Semarang and Surabaya in October (Semarang from 14 October); the Battle of Surabaya ran from 27 October to 2 December 1945. The Dutch 'did not return as a significant force until early 1946'. Reviewer fix: mirrors the dutch-east-indies contest.

1946: the Yogyakarta page says the city 'became the capital of the Indonesian Republic from 1946 to 1948'; the Revolution page says the Dutch landed at Jakarta with British help and 'could not hold the city', so 'The Republican leadership thus established themselves in the city of Yogyakarta'. Neither page gives a day or month, so none is set (a reviewer's 4 January 1946 is on neither page).

region.text: Java, Madura and Sumatra: the Netherlands recognised 'the Republic as the de facto authority over Java, Madura, and Sumatra' (with all of Aceh, which Cliopatria cuts out of its 1946 shape)

ledger.note: 1946: the Netherlands recognises the Republic's de facto authority over Java, Madura and Sumatra in the Linggadjati Agreement, 'concluded in November 1946' (the Dutch Lower House ratified a stripped-down version on 25 March 1947, which the Republic rejected). The Dutch East Indies dossier records the matching loss and the city enclaves held by the Dutch and British in 1945-46. Reviewer fix: Aceh is added to the region. Aceh page: 'The ulama won, and the area remained free during the Indonesian War of Independence' and 'The Dutch military itself never attempted to invade Aceh' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aceh).

region.text: Jakarta, Medan, Padang, Palembang, Semarang and Surabaya, the Republican cities where British forces, with Dutch NICA troops, landed (mirrors dutch-east-indies /ledger/97 and /ledger/99)

ledger.note: November 1946: the Linggadjati Agreement, 'brokered by the British and concluded in November 1946', recognises the Republic as the de facto authority over Java, Madura and Sumatra and ends the first phase. Reviewer fix: mirrors the dutch-east-indies contest.

region.text: parts of Sumatra, and East and West Java, from which 'Dutch forces drove Republican troops out' in Operation Product; the region is the difference between Cliopatria's 1946 and 1947 Republic shapes (Aceh, which the Dutch never invaded, is left out)

ledger.note: 1947: Operation Product begins ('At midnight on 20 July 1947'; the infobox table gives 21 July to 5 August).

region.text: parts of Sumatra, and East and West Java, from which 'Dutch forces drove Republican troops out' in Operation Product; the region is the difference between Cliopatria's 1946 and 1947 Republic shapes (Aceh, which the Dutch never invaded, is left out)

ledger.note: 1947: Operation Product takes the plantation and port regions, held at the ceasefire of 4 August. 'At midnight on 20 July 1947' the Dutch drove Republican troops out of 'parts of Sumatra, and East and West Java' (the infobox table gives 21 July to 5 August); the ceasefire of 4 August 1947 followed under UNSC Resolution 27, and the Renville line was fixed in January 1948.

region.text: parts of Sumatra, and East and West Java, from which 'Dutch forces drove Republican troops out' in Operation Product; the region is the difference between Cliopatria's 1946 and 1947 Republic shapes (Aceh, which the Dutch never invaded, is left out)

ledger.note: 1947: the ceasefire of 4 August 1947 under UN Security Council Resolution 27 ends the offensive; the Renville Agreement of January 1948 froze the Van Mook line.

region.text: the Republic's remaining Java (Yogyakarta, taken 'by the following day') and most of Sumatra, lost in Operation Kraai; the Emergency Government held on in West Sumatra; the region is the difference between Cliopatria's 1948 shape and the 1949 pocket plus West Sumatra and Aceh (which the Dutch never invaded)

ledger.note: 1948: Operation Kraai (19 December) takes Yogyakarta, 'By the following day it had conquered the city of Yogyakarta'; the president and vice-president are captured and exiled to Bangka; the Emergency Government 'was established in West Sumatra' (undated on the page). Cliopatria's pocket starts in 1949. Page, same article: "By the end of December, all major Republican held cities in Java and Sumatra were in Dutch hands" and "An emergency Republican government ... was established in West Sumatra". fx-27 review: counterpart kept as the slug dutch-east-indies. The Dutch East Indies' own December 1948 gain from the Republic (its ledger/105, 902 cells) covers 719 of this loss's 720 cells, so the paired-gain rule already moves the land; the 1950 snap came from the 1949 keyframe, not from this event.

region.text: the Republic's remaining Java (Yogyakarta, taken 'by the following day') and most of Sumatra, lost in Operation Kraai; the Emergency Government held on in West Sumatra; the region is the difference between Cliopatria's 1948 shape and the 1949 pocket plus West Sumatra and Aceh (which the Dutch never invaded)

ledger.note: 1948: Operation Kraai begins (19 December); the Dutch conquer Yogyakarta by the next day.
19 December 1948: with Yogyakarta invaded in Operation Kraai the capital 'was moved to Bukittinggi' (Yogyakarta page), where the Emergency Government was set up in West Sumatra.

region.text: the Yogyakarta region, from which 'the final Dutch forces left ... on 30 June' 1949 under the Roem-Van Roijen Agreement of 7 May 1949 (the admin1 is the researcher's reading of 'the Yogyakarta region')

ledger.note: Roem-Van Roijen page: the agreement 'was an agreement made between Indonesian republicans and the Netherlands on 7 May 1949' (Indonesian forces to 'cease all guerrilla activities', Republican government restored in Yogyakarta) and 'the final Dutch forces left the Yogyakarta region on 30 June'; the Yogyakarta page says 'On 29 June 1949 Yogyakarta was completely cleared of Dutch forces, under pressure from the United Nations'. The rest of the December 1948 zone stays contested to 27 December 1949. dutch-east-indies (se-03) has no matching loss.

6 July 1949: 'republican leaders Sukarno and Hatta returned to the capital' (Roem-Van Roijen page), i.e. Yogyakarta, restored to the Republican government by the agreement; the pages give no month for the return to Jakarta.

region.text: West Java, where Kartosoewirjo proclaimed the Islamic State of Indonesia on 7 August 1949 'in protest against the Renville Agreement'; 'the Darul Islam controlled one-third of West Java' in 1957. The 70 km circle around Garut (where he was captured) cut to West Java is the researcher's reading of 'one-third'

ledger.note: 1949: Darul Islam rises in West Java. Kartosoewirjo proclaims the Islamic State of Indonesia on 7 August 1949 'in protest against the Renville Agreement, which ceded West Java to the Dutch'; the page gives no area before 1957.

1949: the Republic becomes the Republic of the United States of Indonesia. 'Sovereignty was formally transferred on 27 December 1949' to a 'seven-state, nine-territory' federation in which the Republic of Java and Sumatra was one state with almost half the population.

minus.text: western New Guinea, kept by the Netherlands

region.text: all former Dutch East Indies territory except western New Guinea, which 'the Netherlands kept for further talks'

ledger.note: 1949: the Netherlands transfers sovereignty (27 December) over all of the Dutch East Indies except Dutch New Guinea, ending the Revolution (17 August 1945 to 27 December 1949, infobox).

region.text: the Republic's remaining Java (Yogyakarta, taken 'by the following day') and most of Sumatra, lost in Operation Kraai; the Emergency Government held on in West Sumatra; the region is the difference between Cliopatria's 1948 shape and the 1949 pocket plus West Sumatra and Aceh (which the Dutch never invaded)

ledger.note: 1949: the fighting ends with the transfer of sovereignty (27 December 1949; the page dates the Round Table Conference 23 August to 2 November 1949 and gives no cease-fire date for 1949).

1950: the federation becomes a unitary republic (17 August). 'The other fifteen states and territories were dissolved into the Republic in the first half of 1950' (Revolution page); the Indonesia page: the federal state 'was replaced by a unitary republic on 17 August 1950'.

region.text: South Sulawesi, where Abdul Kahar Muzakkar's rebels joined Darul Islam in 1951 and controlled more than 90 percent in 1957

ledger.note: 1951: Kahar Muzakkar's rebels in South Sulawesi join Darul Islam ('joined the Darul Islam movement in 1951'); the page gives no month.

region.text: Aceh, which Daud Beureu'eh declared part of the Islamic State of Indonesia on 20 September 1953; Darul Islam 'controlled more than 90%' of it in 1957, the government holding the towns

ledger.note: 1953: Aceh rises. On 20 September 1953 Daud Beureu'eh declared Aceh part of the Islamic State of Indonesia under Kartosoewirjo; martial law was imposed in 1957.

region.text: the regions the PRRI page names as PRRI's (Tapanuli, West Sumatra, Riau, Jambi, South Sumatra: Tapanuli is the 80 km circle at Padangsidempuan) and North Sulawesi, where the Permesta rebels who pledged allegiance to the PRRI took over local government; the pages give no extent of land actually held

ledger.note: 15 February 1958: 'The PRRI was proclaimed to have been established on 15 February 1958 by Lieutenant Colonel Ahmad Hussein' (infobox: 17 February); the Permesta rebels, founded on 2 March 1957 (Permesta page), 'had pledged allegiance with the PRRI on 17 February 1958'. The page lists Tapanuli, West Sumatra, Riau, Jambi and South Sumatra as PRRI regions and gives no dates for the government's counter-operations; 'Manado was captured at the end of June 1958' (Permesta page). The region is the named provinces, not the land held.

region.text: the regions the PRRI page names as PRRI's (Tapanuli, West Sumatra, Riau, Jambi, South Sumatra: Tapanuli is the 80 km circle at Padangsidempuan) and North Sulawesi, where the Permesta rebels who pledged allegiance to the PRRI took over local government; the pages give no extent of land actually held

ledger.note: 28 September 1961: the infobox lists the PRRI government's disestablishment; the Permesta page says its last remnants 'surrendered and were given amnesty in 1961' (Kawilarang surrendered on 14 April 1961, Sumual on 20 October 1961, and the last commander, Kumontoy, in early 1962).

region.text: Aceh, which Daud Beureu'eh declared part of the Islamic State of Indonesia on 20 September 1953; Darul Islam 'controlled more than 90%' of it in 1957, the government holding the towns

ledger.note: 1962: peace in Aceh. 'Three years of negotiations (1959-1962) produced a peace agreement' that restored Aceh as an autonomous province with special rights for Islamic law; Cliopatria ends its Aceh row in 1959.

region.text: the Merauke coast of West New Guinea, where on 24 June 1962 four C-130s 'dropped 213 paratroopers near Merauke'; the radius is the researcher's reading

ledger.note: 1962: Indonesian paratroopers land near Merauke (24 June) after Sukarno's order of 19 December 1961 to prepare an invasion; 'The Dutch retained control over their colony on the western half of New Guinea' since 1949.

region.text: the Merauke coast of West New Guinea, where on 24 June 1962 four C-130s 'dropped 213 paratroopers near Merauke'; the radius is the researcher's reading

ledger.note: 1962: the New York Agreement (15 August) ends the fighting; the Dutch are to hand West New Guinea to the UN on 1 October 1962.

region.text: West Java, where Kartosoewirjo proclaimed the Islamic State of Indonesia on 7 August 1949 'in protest against the Renville Agreement'; 'the Darul Islam controlled one-third of West Java' in 1957. The 70 km circle around Garut (where he was captured) cut to West Java is the researcher's reading of 'one-third'

ledger.note: 1962: Darul Islam ends in West Java. Kartosoewirjo was captured on 4 June 1962 near Garut and executed; 'the last Darul Islam band in West Java surrendered in August 1962'.

region.text: western New Guinea (Papua and West Papua), transferred by UNTEA to Indonesia on 1 May 1963

ledger.note: 1963: UNTEA hands West New Guinea to Indonesia (1 May). 'The Act of Free Choice in 1969 formalised Indonesian rule' (Indonesia page; the dispute page gives only the year). The Dutch had held it since 1949.

region.text: South Sulawesi, where Abdul Kahar Muzakkar's rebels joined Darul Islam in 1951 and controlled more than 90 percent in 1957

ledger.note: 1965: the last Darul Islam rising ends. Kahar Muzakkar was killed in an ambush in February 1965 in the interior of Southeast Sulawesi.

region.text: East Timor, invaded on 7 December 1975 in Operasi Seroja, 'the largest military operation ever carried out by that nation'

ledger.note: 1975: Indonesia invades East Timor (7 December), nine days after Fretilin declared independence on 28 November; Batugade fell on 8 October and Balibo on about 16 October. The Portuguese colony is the Estado Novo's Cliopatria shape to 1975.

region.text: East Timor, annexed as Indonesia's 27th province

ledger.note: 1976: the contest ends in annexation (17 July); resistance continues, and the UN keeps Portugal as administering power (the infobox gives a de jure occupation to 20 May 2002).

region.text: East Timor, annexed as Indonesia's 27th province

ledger.note: 1976: Indonesia annexes East Timor (17 July): 'Indonesia formally annexed East Timor as its 27th province'. Only Australia besides Indonesia recognised it.

region.text: East Timor after the 30 August 1999 referendum (78.5 percent for independence); INTERFET entered Dili on 20 September and 'By 31 October 1999, the last Indonesian troops had left East Timor'

ledger.note: 1999: Indonesia leaves East Timor. The territory is administered by the UN (UNTAET, 'at the end of October') until independence on 20 May 2002; Cliopatria's East Timor row starts only in 2006.

wars.name: Indonesian National Revolution

zones.text: Jakarta, Medan, Padang, Palembang, Semarang and Surabaya, the Republican cities where British forces, with Dutch NICA troops, landed (mirrors dutch-east-indies /ledger/97 and /ledger/99)

parts of Sumatra, and East and West Java, from which 'Dutch forces drove Republican troops out' in Operation Product; the region is the difference between Cliopatria's 1946 and 1947 Republic shapes (Aceh, which the Dutch never invaded, is left out)

the Republic's remaining Java (Yogyakarta, taken 'by the following day') and most of Sumatra, lost in Operation Kraai; the Emergency Government held on in West Sumatra; the region is the difference between Cliopatria's 1948 shape and the 1949 pocket plus West Sumatra and Aceh (which the Dutch never invaded)

wars.outcome: The Netherlands transferred sovereignty on 27 December 1949 over the whole Dutch East Indies except western New Guinea after two offensives (Operation Product, July 1947; Operation Kraai, December 1948) and the Renville Agreement (January 1948).
wars.note: Infobox 17 August 1945 to 27 December 1949. Round Table Conference in The Hague, 23 August to 2 November 1949.

wars.name: Darul Islam rebellion

zones.text: West Java, where Kartosoewirjo proclaimed the Islamic State of Indonesia on 7 August 1949 'in protest against the Renville Agreement'; 'the Darul Islam controlled one-third of West Java' in 1957. The 70 km circle around Garut (where he was captured) cut to West Java is the researcher's reading of 'one-third'
Aceh, which Daud Beureu'eh declared part of the Islamic State of Indonesia on 20 September 1953; Darul Islam 'controlled more than 90%' of it in 1957, the government holding the towns
South Sulawesi, where Abdul Kahar Muzakkar's rebels joined Darul Islam in 1951 and controlled more than 90 percent in 1957

wars.outcome: The rebellion ended region by region: South Kalimantan in 1959, Aceh by negotiated peace (1959-1962), West Java in June-August 1962, South Sulawesi in February 1965.
wars.note: In 1957 the page estimates Darul Islam held one-third of West Java and more than 90 percent of Aceh and of South Sulawesi. Permesta and the PRRI (1957-58) are not on the page.

wars.name: PRRI and Permesta rebellion

zones.text: the regions the PRRI page names as PRRI's (Tapanuli, West Sumatra, Riau, Jambi, South Sumatra: Tapanuli is the 80 km circle at Padangsidempuan) and North Sulawesi, where the Permesta rebels who pledged allegiance to the PRRI took over local government; the pages give no extent of land actually held

wars.outcome: The PRRI government was disestablished on 28 September 1961 (infobox) and the last Permesta remnants surrendered and were given amnesty in 1961, the last commander in early 1962.
wars.note: Proclaimed 15 February 1958 (infobox 17 February); Permesta pledged allegiance on 17 February 1958. The pages give no extent of the land held and no dates for the government's counter-operations.

wars.name: West New Guinea dispute

zones.text: the Merauke coast of West New Guinea, where on 24 June 1962 four C-130s 'dropped 213 paratroopers near Merauke'; the radius is the researcher's reading

wars.outcome: Operation Trikora (ordered 19 December 1961) and the 1962 infiltrations led to the New York Agreement (15 August 1962), UNTEA (planned from 1 October 1962) and the transfer to Indonesia on 1 May 1963.
wars.note: Operation Jayawijaya, planned for around August 1962, was cancelled on 17 August 1962.

wars.name: Indonesian occupation of East Timor
wars.outcome: Indonesia invaded (7 December 1975), annexed East Timor (17 July 1976) and withdrew after the 30 August 1999 referendum; independence 20 May 2002.
wars.note: Infobox: occupation 7 December 1975 to 31 October 1999; de jure to 20 May 2002.

wars.name: Free Aceh Movement insurgency
wars.outcome: Hasan di Tiro founded GAM and declared independence in 1976; the insurgency revived in 1989, prompting a decade-long military campaign; the Yudhoyono administration 'reached a peace agreement with Aceh separatists in 2005'.
wars.note: The page gives no territory held by GAM, so no zone.

certainty.note: The Revolution's fronts moved with each offensive and the Van Mook line was 'an artificial line which connected the most advanced Dutch tanks' positions'; Republican guerrilla zones behind the Dutch lines are not mapped by the pages.

Judgment: a recognised state with surveyed land and treaty maritime borders; no page opened dates the boundary agreements. The rebel zones of 1949-1965 and the East Timor frontier of 1975-1999 were contested lines, soft in the contest events.

notes: Page budget (5) was spent in the first run; the review fixes opened five more pages on the reviewer's instruction (Aceh, Yogyakarta, Roem-Van Roijen, Permesta, PRRI). Cliopatria rows: the 1950, 1953 and 1960 shapes include western New Guinea (Papua and West Papua) until 1962, wrong because the Netherlands kept it to 1 May 1963; the 1976 shape includes East Timor to 2005 though Indonesia left in October 1999; the 1949 shape is a Riau and Jambi pocket that omits West Sumatra, where the Emergency Government sat. Cliopatria's Sultanate of Aceh rows (1946-1948 and 1953-1959) overlay land that the Republic held or fought over; the sultanate-of-aceh dossier (se-02) marks those rows wrong and says they belong here: Aceh is now added to keyframes 1945, 1946, 1947, 1949 and 1953, to the founding and 1946 gain regions, and left out of the Operation Product and Kraai contest zones because the Dutch never invaded it. Recorded after review: the Roem-Van Roijen agreement (7 May 1949) and the Dutch withdrawal from Yogyakarta (30 June 1949; the Yogyakarta page says 29 June), the capital's move to Bukittinggi (19 December 1948) and back (6 July 1949), the PRRI and Permesta rebellion (contest 1958-02 to 1961-09, regions only). Still not on the pages and therefore not recorded: the dates of the Dutch-sponsored federal states (the page gives East Indonesia in December 1946, South Sumatra and East Java by July 1948, Pasundan), the day of the move to Yogyakarta in January 1946 (the Yogyakarta page says only 1946 to 1948), the extent of the land the PRRI and Permesta actually held and the dates of the government's counter-operations, the Republic's return to Jakarta, and the Aceh special-region status. South Kalimantan (Ibnu Hadjar's Darul Islam forces 'were forced to surrender in 1959'; the page gives no start) is not recorded as a contest because the pairing needs a dated start. Contest zones against negara-islam-indonesia are the Darul Islam areas of 1957 (one third of West Java, over 90 percent of Aceh and South Sulawesi): the extent in other years is not on the page. No rulers list: the Indonesia page names Sukarno (from 1945), Suharto (de facto control from 1966, resigned May 1998), Yudhoyono (2004 election), Widodo (2014), Prabowo (2024) without reign years. Counterparts needing dossiers: negara-islam-indonesia (written here as a rebel state), dutch-new-guinea (1949-1963), east-timor from 1975 (the Cliopatria row starts 2006) and the PRRI/Permesta rebels (revolutionary-government-of-the-republic-of-indonesia, 1957-1961, used as the counterpart of ledger 1958-02 and 1961-09).
